passage: Himani, you asked what happens when I have to speak in class. Here's the inside view. My heart starts pounding before "Kishore" is even called. My face goes hot; I can feel it turning red, which makes it redder. Then my mind goes blank, even if I studied. Afterwards I replay every second on the bus home: the pause, the wobble, the one kid who smirked. For months I just avoided it. I'd take the zero for oral work and feel so relieved. But the fear got bigger, not smaller. So with the counsellor I've made a ladder: first, reading one line to her; then answering one yes-or-no question in class; then, one day, the whole presentation. Yesterday I did step two.

qa.q: Which step of the ladder did Kishore do yesterday?
qa.a: Kishore did step two.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel after taking the zero for oral work?
qa.a: So relieved at the time, though the fear kept getting bigger.

qa.q: What plan did Kishore make with the counsellor, and why does it help?
qa.a: A ladder of small steps, from reading one line to the whole presentation, so the fear shrinks through gentle practice instead of avoidance.

qa.q: What might Himani understand after hearing the inside view?
qa.a: Himani may realise that Kishore's silence in class comes from a pounding heart and a blank mind, not from not studying.

grounding: A teenager describes a racing heart, blushing and a blank mind before speaking, the relief and cost of avoiding, and a gentle step-by-step plan with a counsellor.

passage:
I sit next to Madhav in Hindi class, so I see it up close. When the teacher says, "Madhav, read the next paragraph," his ears go red first, then his neck. His hand grips the book so tight the page crinkles. He reads the first line, stops, and stares at the words as if they've turned into another language. He sits down, and for the rest of the period he doesn't look up. Last month he stopped coming on Fridays, when we have recitation. I don't know what he's thinking; he never says. But this week the teacher started letting him read sitting down, one line, then two. On Friday he came. He read four lines. His ears were still red. He finished anyway.
Yusuf

qa.q: What happens to Madhav's ears when he is asked to read?
qa.a: His ears go red first, then his neck.

qa.q: What might Madhav's staring at the words suggest he feels, given Yusuf can't be sure?
qa.a: It suggests his mind has gone blank with fear, even though the words are familiar.

qa.q: What change did the teacher make, and what happened?
qa.a: The teacher let him read sitting down, one line then two, and on Friday he came and read four lines.

qa.q: How might Yusuf feel watching Madhav finish four lines?
qa.a: Yusuf may feel glad and quietly proud of him, having seen up close how hard it was.

grounding: A classmate watches a boy blush and blank when asked to read, avoid recitation days, and then return through gentle small steps.

passage: Every time Pablo had to speak in class at his London school, his body went off like an alarm: heart racing, face burning red, mind wiped white. In October he stood up to present on volcanoes and forgot his second sentence. He replayed it every night for a week. So when the next presentation came, he stayed home with a stomach ache. The relief was huge, for about a day. Then the fear of the next one grew bigger. His form tutor sent him to Ms. Nkechi Obi, the school counsellor. She didn't tell him to just be brave. Together they made a ladder: read one line to her; then to two friends; then ask one question in class. 'Your body is trying to protect you,' she said. 'We'll teach it, slowly.' In December Pablo asked one question in geography. His face went red. He asked it anyway.

qa.q: What was Pablo's October presentation about?
qa.a: Volcanoes.

qa.q: How did Pablo feel after staying home from the next presentation?
qa.a: He felt huge relief for about a day, then the fear of the next one grew bigger.

qa.q: Why is Ms. Obi's ladder better than staying home?
qa.a: Small, gentle steps with support teach his body it can cope, while avoiding only made the fear larger.

qa.q: How does Ms. Obi see Pablo's racing heart and blushing?
qa.a: She sees them as his body trying to protect him, something to retrain slowly, not a weakness.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose body reacts strongly before speaking, who finds avoidance brings brief relief but bigger fear, and who improves with gentle, supported steps.

passage: At basketball practice, Coach Alka told Gargi she would give the team talk before the zonal match. Gargi's heart began to race right there on the court. By evening she had a plan: be sick on match day. The thought felt like relief. Coach Alka caught her at the water cooler. 'You went red as a tomato when I said it. Talk to me.' Gargi blurted it out: the blushing, the blank mind, the way she replayed every word for days. 'And if I skip it, I'm fine.' 'For a day,' said Coach Alka. 'Then the next talk feels twice as big. How about this: tomorrow, one sentence to me. Thursday, to the three starters. Saturday, the whole team, with notes.' Gargi swallowed. 'And if my face goes red?' 'Then it goes red, and you keep talking.'

qa.q: What was Gargi supposed to give before the zonal match?
qa.a: The team talk.

qa.q: What did Gargi feel when she planned to be sick on match day?
qa.a: She felt relief, as if skipping would make the fear go away.

qa.q: What steps did Coach Alka suggest?
qa.a: One sentence to the coach tomorrow, then to the three starters on Thursday, then the whole team on Saturday with notes: gentle, supported exposure.

qa.q: How did Coach Alka read Gargi's red face?
qa.a: Coach Alka noticed a player struggling and chose to talk and help, rather than let her quietly avoid the talk.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose racing heart, blushing and blank mind push her to avoid speaking, and a coach who offers gentle, step-by-step practice instead.

passage:
Dear Vidya Didi,
You asked me to write when I tried the first step, so here it is. You know what happens to me: before I talk in front of people, my heart pounds, my face goes hot, and my head empties like a tipped bucket. Afterwards I replay every word like a crime.
For two years I just avoided things. Every time I skipped, I felt better that night and worse the next month.
This week, as we planned with the school counsellor, I did step one: I read out the attendance list in chemistry. My voice wobbled on the third name. My face was on fire. Then it was over, nobody said anything, and Rafiq asked me for a pen like normal.
I replayed it only twice. Step two is next Tuesday. I'm scared. I'm going anyway.
Akash

qa.q: What did Akash read out in chemistry?
qa.a: The attendance list.

qa.q: How does Akash feel about step two?
qa.a: Akash is scared but determined to go anyway.

qa.q: Why is reading the attendance list a good first step?
qa.a: It is a small, manageable step planned with the counsellor, showing Akash that the feared moment passes and nobody reacts.

qa.q: How might Vidya feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Vidya would probably feel proud and encouraged, seeing Akash take a first step after two years of avoiding.

grounding: Shows a teenager who describes the racing heart and blank mind before speaking, sees that avoidance made fear larger, and starts gentle steps with help.

passage:
You want to know why I never answer in class? Okay, Nitin, I'll tell you. I'm Ritu, and I know the answers, all right.
But the second Ma'am looks my way, my heart starts pounding, my face goes hot and red, and my head goes totally blank. Like someone switched off a light.
If I do say something, I replay it all evening. The wobble in my voice. The one wrong word. It feels like a disaster.
So I stopped raising my hand. And yes, that felt good at first, such relief. But then the fear got bigger. Now even reading my name on the attendance list feels scary.
Last week I told Ma'am. She said we'd start small: I read one line from my seat, only on days I choose. Yesterday I did it. My heart still pounded. But I got through the line, and nobody laughed.

qa.q: What did Ma'am suggest Ritu do to start?
qa.a: Read one line from Ritu's seat, only on days Ritu chooses.

qa.q: How does Ritu feel after speaking in class, and what shows it?
qa.a: Ritu feels embarrassed and anxious, replaying the wobble and the wrong word all evening as if it were a disaster.

qa.q: Why was telling Ma'am a better step than staying silent?
qa.a: Staying silent brought relief but made the fear bigger; telling Ma'am led to small, chosen steps with help, which let Ritu get through a line.

qa.q: How might Nitin see Ritu differently after hearing this?
qa.a: Nitin might realise Ritu's silence is not lack of knowledge but fear, and could be more patient and encouraging in class.

grounding: Shows a teen whose racing heart and blank mind before speaking lead to avoidance, and how small steps with a teacher's help work better.
